provider_query: The first YouTube video, Me at the zoo
answer:
**“Me at the zoo”** is the first video uploaded to YouTube. Co-founder **Jawed Karim** posted the 19-second clip on April 23, 2005 (about 8:27–8:32 p.m. PDT), on the channel “jawed.”

Relevant facts:

1. **What it shows** — Karim stands in front of two elephants at the San Diego Zoo and says they have “really, really, really long” trunks. His high school friend **Yakov Lapitsky** filmed it. [web:0] [web:8]

2. **Direct link** — Still online: [youtube.com/watch?v=jNQXAC9IVRw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNQXAC9IVRw). Recent listings put views around 350–440 million, with tens of millions of likes. [web:4] [web:1]

3. **Why it exists** — It was mainly a tech test of the new site. Karim has said difficulty finding clips online (including the 2004 Super Bowl halftime incident) helped inspire a simple video-sharing site with Chad Hurley and Steve Chen. [web:1] [web:6]

4. **Legacy** — Often called YouTube’s first vlog and a milestone of user-generated video. *The New York Observer* and *BuzzFeed News* have ranked it among the most important videos in the platform’s history. [web:0] [web:8]

5. **Zoo reaction** — The official San Diego Zoo channel later commented that it was honored the first YouTube video was filmed there; that comment became one of the most-liked on YouTube. [web:3] [web:12]

6. **20-year mark** — Coverage in April 2025 treated the clip as the start of YouTube’s history, noting hundreds of millions of views and its role in short, casual video. [web:1] [web:7]

7. **Background** — Domain registered February 2005; Google bought YouTube in 2006 for $1.65 billion. The clip is still cited as the origin point of that trajectory. [web:5]

8. **Description edits** — Karim has occasionally changed the description (including joke or protest links); the video itself remains the original short zoo clip. [web:3] [web:7]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

First video uploaded to YouTube

This article is about the YouTube video. For the 2012 film, see _Me at the Zoo_ (2012 film) "Me at the Zoo (2012 film)").

| "Me at the zoo" |

| Video 1 The full YouTube video "Me at the zoo" |
| Produced by | Jawed Karim |
| Starring | Jawed Karim |
| Cinematography | Yakov Lapitsky |
| Release date |  April 23,2005(2005-04-23) 8:31 p.m. PDT |
| Running time | 20 seconds |
| Country | United States |
| Language | English |

"Me at the zoo" is a YouTube video uploaded on April 23, 2005, recognized as the first video uploaded to the platform. The 19-second video features Jawed Karim, one of the co-founders of YouTube, being recorded by his high school friend, Yakov Lapitsky. In the video, Karim is seen standing in front of two elephants at the San Diego Zoo in California, where he briefly comments on the length of their trunks.Multiple journalists have opined that the video represented YouTube as a whole and stated it was a milestone of the platform's history. Karim has later updated the video's description several times. As of September 2026, the video has received more than 416 million views.(

## Background

[edit]

Further information: YouTube §Founding and initial growth (2005–2006) "YouTube")

Image 5

Elephants at the San Diego Zoo in 2013, where "Me at the zoo" was filmed

YouTube was founded in 2005 by three former PayPal employees – Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim. Hurley studied design at the Indiana University of Pennsylvania, while Chen studied computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.( Karim stated that inspiration for the platform came from the Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show controversy and the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami.( He was unable to find video clips of these events online, which gave him the idea to start a video-sharing website.(

## Release

[edit]

"Me at the zoo" was uploaded on April 23, 2005,( at 8:31:52 p.m. PDT( It shows Karim at the San Diego Zoo in California, in front of two elephants. In the 19-second video, he notes the length of their trunks.( His high school friend Yakov Lapitsky recorded the video.( In it, Karim states:

> Alright, so here we are in front of the, uh, elephants, and the cool thing about these guys is that, is that they have really, really, really long, um, trunks, and that's – that's cool. And that's pretty much all there is to say.(

## Retrospective reception

[edit]

Multiple publications agreed that the video embodies YouTube as a whole. _Business Insider_ ranked it the most important YouTube video of all time, stating that it is emblematic of YouTube's user-generated nature.( New York Observer_ also ranked it as the most important video in YouTube history, noting its historical significance.( News_ listed it among the 20 most important online videos of all time.( As the first video on YouTube, it has also been described as the first YouTube vlog.(

Reviewers thought that "Me at the zoo" was a monumental part of YouTube's history. Aaron Duplantier, in his book _Authenticity and How We Fake It: Belief and Subjectivity in Reality TV, Facebook and YouTube_, stated that the ordinary nature of "Me at the zoo" set the tone for the type of original, amateur content that would become typical of YouTube, especially among YouTubers and vloggers.( The _Los Angeles Times_ explained in 2009 that "Me at the zoo" made a significant change in how media was consumed, establishing an era of short videos.( Trends_ deemed it set a standard for future videos on YouTube.( Film critic Peter Bradshaw listed the video as one of the key releases of the 2000s.(The official San Diego Zoo YouTube account left a now-pinned comment on the video in 2020, stating "We're so honored that the first ever YouTube video was filmed here!"( As of April 22, 2026, it is the most-liked comment on the platform, with 4.5 million likes.( In February 2026, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London acquired a reconstructed early webpage and the "Me at the zoo" video, built by the museum's digital conservation team over 18 months.(

## Changes to original video

[edit]

Karim has repeatedly used the video's description to criticize YouTube's business actions. In response to Google requiring YouTube users to use Google+ accounts to comment on videos, he updated the description in November 2013 to say, "why the fuck do i need a google+ account to comment on a video?"( He changed the video's description again in November 2021 in response to YouTube's decision to remove video dislikes from public view, stating, "When every YouTuber agrees that removing dislikes is a stupid idea, it probably is. Try again, YouTube."( A few days later, he again updated the description to include a longer condemnation of YouTube's decision.( On December 16, 2023, the video thumbnail was changed to a MrBeast-style image of Karim with fiery eyes and pointing at a background image of stampeding elephants. It was reverted to the original thumbnail two weeks later.( In February 2025, Karim updated the description to refer to the danger of microplastics to the brain.( The description also contains timestamps for chapters: "Intro", "The cool thing", and "End".

# The history of YouTube: from a zoo video to TV giant

On this page8 sections

At a glance

- Three former PayPal employees founded YouTube in 2005, and its first video was 19 seconds at the San Diego Zoo
- Google bought it for $1.65 billion in 2006, a deal many thought was too expensive
- Today YouTube is the most watched streaming service on US televisions, with about 14% of all TV viewing in July 2026

* * *

YouTube is so familiar that it is hard to remember the internet without it. But in early 2005 there was no easy way to share a video online. Three former PayPal employees set out to fix that, and in less than two years they sold their startup to Google. Two decades later, YouTube is the most watched streaming service on American televisions, a music and TV subscription business, and the home of a creator economy that did not exist when it launched. Here is how a 19-second clip grew into one of the world's biggest entertainment platforms, and why each turn happened.

### 2005: three founders and a zoo

Chad Hurley, Steve Chen and Jawed Karim registered the YouTube domain in February 2005. Their offices were above a pizzeria in San Mateo, California. On April 23, 2005, Karim uploaded the first video, "Me at the zoo," in which he stands in front of the elephants at the San Diego Zoo and talks about their long trunks. It is still online and has been watched hundreds of millions of times.

YouTube's breakthrough was simplicity. Uploading video in 2005 usually meant wrestling with file formats and plug-ins, and viewers often had to download a file before they could watch it. YouTube converted videos into a format that played in any web browser and let anyone embed them on other sites, including the blogs and MySpace pages that were popular at the time. Every embed was free advertising, and within a year the site was serving tens of millions of videos a day.

![Walt Mossberg interviewing YouTube co-founders Steve Chen and Chad Hurley on red chairs on a blue-lit stage](https://applescoop.org/image/story/chad-hurley-steve-chen-youtube-founders-inline-2026-10-13.jpg)_Photo via Wikimedia Commons // YouTube co-founders Steve Chen, center, and Chad Hurley, right, interviewed on stage by Walt Mossberg._

### 2006: Google pays $1.65 billion

In October 2006, Google agreed to buy YouTube for $1.65 billion in stock. Google already had its own service, Google Video, but it was losing to YouTube's community and ease of use, and buying the leader was faster than catching up. Many observers still thought Google was overpaying for a site that made little money, paid enormous bandwidth bills and faced lawsuits over copyrighted clips, including a high-profile case brought by Viacom.

Google's answer was Content ID, launched in 2007. It lets rights holders upload reference files, automatically find matching uploads and choose whether to block them, track them or run ads and keep the revenue. That turned a legal problem into a revenue stream for studios and labels, and it is a big reason music companies came to treat YouTube as a partner rather than an enemy. Our [history of Google](https://applescoop.org/story/google-history-timeline-garage-search-android-gemini) puts the deal alongside the company's other big bets, such as Android.

Explore Apple Scoop [Find your next wallpaper →](https://applescoop.org/wallpapers/) [Read the latest Apple news →](https://applescoop.org/)

YouTube was also built into the first iPhone in 2007 as one of its original apps, a sign of how central online video had already become. Apple wrote that app itself, and YouTube re-encoded videos into the H.264 format the iPhone could play without Flash.

### The creator economy

In 2007 YouTube launched its Partner Program, sharing advertising revenue with the people who made videos. That created a new kind of career. Gamers, beauty experts, comedians and teachers built audiences larger than many TV channels, and YouTube began awarding Play Buttons to channels that reached 100,000, 1 million and 10 million subscribers.

The revenue split is why YouTube kept its creators when rivals offered bigger audiences or slicker apps. Creators generally receive the majority of ad revenue from long videos, and multichannel networks, brand deals, memberships and merchandise grew around that base. The scale became enormous: Alphabet reported more than $36 billion in YouTube ad revenue for 2024 alone.

![A framed YouTube Silver Play Button award standing upright in sand on a beach](https://applescoop.org/image/story/youtube-silver-play-button-award-inline-2026-10-13.jpg)_Photo via Wikimedia Commons // A YouTube Silver Play Button, awarded to channels that pass 100,000 subscribers._

### The Wojcicki years

Susan Wojcicki, one of Google's earliest employees, became YouTube's CEO in 2014. She led its expansion into paid services, including YouTube Music and YouTube Premium for ad-free viewing, and YouTube TV, a live TV service launched in 2017. Subscriptions gave YouTube a second business that did not depend on advertisers, and YouTube said in 2025 that Music and Premium had passed 125 million subscribers, including trials.

She also faced difficult years over misinformation, extremist content and child safety. Advertisers paused spending in 2017 after their ads appeared beside extremist videos, and a 2019 settlement with US regulators over children's data led to tighter rules for content aimed at children. Those episodes pushed YouTube toward stricter monetization rules, more human review and clearer labels on content made for kids.

![Susan Wojcicki sitting in a director's chair on a set talking with the hosts of Good Mythical Morning at a desk](https://applescoop.org/image/story/susan-wojcicki-youtube-ceo-vidcon-inline-2026-10-13.jpg)_Photo via Wikimedia Commons // Susan Wojcicki, YouTube's CEO from 2014 to 2023, with the hosts of Good Mythical Morning at VidCon._

Wojcicki stepped down in February 2023 and was succeeded by Neal Mohan. She died in August 2024 at the age of 56.

### Shorts, TV screens and sport

TikTok's success pushed YouTube to launch Shorts, its vertical short-video format, in 2020 and 2021. Shorts now draws hundreds of billions of views a day, and it gave YouTube a defense against [TikTok's rise](https://applescoop.org/story/tiktok-history-timeline-musically-ban-us-joint-venture) that relied on the creators it already had.

At the same time, more people started watching YouTube on televisions instead of phones and laptops. Nielsen's monthly Gauge has regularly ranked YouTube as the most watched streaming service on US TVs, and in July 2026 it accounted for about 14% of all TV viewing, ahead of Netflix. That shift changed what YouTube is: long videos, podcasts and live sport watched from the sofa compete directly with services covered in our [streaming price comparison](https://applescoop.org/story/streaming-service-prices-2026-netflix-disney-hbo-max-compared).

Sport and live events followed the audience. YouTube took over the NFL Sunday Ticket package from the 2023 season, under a deal reported at about $2 billion a year, and in September 2026 it offered the package to Premium subscribers for $204 a year. In December 2025, the Academy announced that the Oscars will stream on YouTube, free worldwide, starting in 2029, a symbol of how far the site has moved from home videos.

Explore Apple Scoop [Find your next wallpaper →](https://applescoop.org/wallpapers/) [Read the latest Apple news →](https://applescoop.org/)

The newest change is AI. On October 13, 2026, Google began rolling out Ask YouTube, a Gemini-powered conversational search that answers questions about videos, to all users of the Android and iPhone apps in the US. It had previously been limited to TVs and Premium subscribers.

### YouTube on Apple devices

YouTube's relationship with Apple has been bumpy. Apple removed its built-in YouTube app in iOS 6 in 2012, after its license to include the app ended, and Google released its own app. Features such as background playback and picture-in-picture on iPhone are still mostly reserved for Premium subscribers, which is a frequent source of frustration for iPhone owners who see those features as standard elsewhere in iOS.

Vision Pro was the longest standoff. For two years Google directed headset owners to Safari, and a popular third-party app, Juno, was removed after a terms-of-service complaint. YouTube finally released a native visionOS app on February 12, 2026, with a Spatial tab for 3D, VR180 and 360-degree videos and 8K playback on the M5 Vision Pro.

For watching on a big screen, Apple's new A19 streaming box, announced on October 13, is covered in our guide to [the new Apple TV 4K](https://applescoop.org/story/new-apple-tv-4k-2026-worth-299-siri-ai-older-models).

### What YouTube's history explains

YouTube won by removing friction, then survived its legal and advertiser crises by building systems, Content ID and the Partner Program, that paid the people whose work it relied on. That combination still defines it. It is also why critics argue that YouTube has become too important to sit inside Google; our look at [the case for splitting up YouTube and Google](https://applescoop.org/story/monopoly-meltdown-the-case-for-splitting-up-youtube-and-google) examines that argument. For more on the parent company, see our [surprising facts about Google](https://applescoop.org/story/50-surprising-facts-about-google-i-bet-you-didnt-know).

# Me at the zoo

| Me at the zoo | |
 --- |
|  | |
| Produced by | Jawed Karim |
| Starring | Jawed Karim |
| Cinematography | Yakov Lapitsky |
| Release date |  23 April 2005 (2005-04-23) |
| Running time | 19 seconds |
| Country | United States |
| Language | English |

Me at the zoo is the first YouTube video. It was uploaded on 23 April 2005, under the username "jawed" by Jawed Karim, one of the founders of YouTube. The 19-second video was recorded by Yakov Lapitsky.

The video showcases his explanation of elephants at the San Diego Zoo.

## Text

Alright, so here we are in front of the, uh, elephants. Uh. The cool thing about these guys is that, is that they have really, really, really long, um, trunks, and that’s, that’s cool. And that’s pretty much all there is to say.

# 20 Years of YouTube: In 2005, a trip to the zoo started it all

By [Sam Gutelle](https://www.tubefilter.com/author/sam-gutelle/)•04/23/2025•

![20 Years of YouTube: In 2005, a trip to the zoo started it all](https://www.tubefilter.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/me-at-the-zoo-youtube-20-1400x825.jpg)

_In [February 2025](https://www.tubefilter.com/2025/02/11/youtube-founded-20-years-ago-february-2005/), YouTube turned 20. The video site has gone through a lot over the past two decades, including an acquisition, an earnings glow-up, and multiple generations of star creators. In our 20 Years of YouTube series, we’ll examine the uploads, trends, and influencers that have defined the world’s favorite video site — one year at a time. [Click here](https://www.tubefilter.com/tag/20-years-of-youtube) for a full archive of the series._

* * *

Over a history that spans more than 100 years, the **San Diego Zoo** has made numerous media appearances. It served as a filming location for Orson Welles’ _Citizen Kane_, provided the cover art for the Beach Boys’ album _Pet Sounds_, and showed up at the climax of the comedy classic _Anchorman_.

But for all of the San Diego Zoo’s memorable moments, its most significant contribution to pop culture may have been a 19-second video recorded in 2005. The facility’s elephant enclosure served as the filming location for “ **me at the zoo**,” the first video ever uploaded to **YouTube**.

![Tubefilter](https://www.tubefilter.com/wp-content/themes/tubefilter/images/logo_main.svg)

### Subscribe for daily Tubefilter Top Stories

Subscribe

When it first hit YouTube on April 23, 2005, “me at the zoo” was little more than a test of the new platform’s technology. The star of the video, YouTube co-founder **Jawed Karim**, seemed to choose a banal setting to avoid distracting from the video’s experimental purpose.

After two decades of twists and turns, Karim’s commentary outside the elephant enclosure has become the stuff of gospel. Some longtime YouTube viewers can recite the clip’s entire script, and it has become one of the most-watched non-music videos in YouTube history, with more than **354 million lifetime views**.

Me at the zoo - YouTube

[Me at the zoo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNQXAC9IVRw) [jawed](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC4QobU6STFB0P71PMvOGN5A)

jawed6.69M subscribers

[Watch on](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNQXAC9IVRw)

Karim may not have predicted it at the time, but “me at the zoo” has come to epitomize several of YouTube’s core characteristics. It is often described as the platform’s [first vlog](https://www.polygon.com/2018/4/23/17272402/first-youtube-video-anniversary-13-jawed-karim), and it emphasized YouTube’s initial focus on short, user-generated videos.

“‘Me at the zoo’ was not a cinematic masterpiece,” Alex Pham wrote in the _Los Angeles Times_ [in 2010](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-may-17-la-et-youtube-20100517-story.html). “But as the first video uploaded to YouTube, it played a pivotal role in fundamentally altering how people consumed media and helped usher in a golden era of the 60-second video.”

These days, Karim’s magnum opus also reflects another aspect of YouTube’s homegrown culture: Its penchant for stirring up drama. The man who founded YouTube alongside **Steve Chen** and **Chad Hurley** occasionally updates “me at the zoo” to use the video as his soapbox for commenting on the latest platform-wide changes.

In 2013, Karim used [his channel](https://www.youtube.com/@jawed) (which features no other videos) to [criticize mandated Google+ integrations on YouTube](https://www.tubefilter.com/2013/11/11/youtube-comments-petition-hank-green-penguinz0-jawed-karim/). Nearly a decade later, he used the description box for “me at the zoo” to [protest the removal of dislikes](https://www.tubefilter.com/2021/11/17/youtube-jawed-karim-dislike-count-protest-me-at-the-zoo/). At the time of this post, the “me at the zoo” description offers information about how “microplastics are accumulating in human brains at an alarming rate.”

20 years after “me at the zoo,” it doesn’t exactly resemble the typical YouTube video — at least not in the way it once did. Karim’s updates, however, still embody the spirit of the platform he launched. YouTube is a content platform, a cultural touchstone, and an entertainment phenomenon, but above all, it’s a hub filled with fierce discussion and debate. Maybe Karim will one day [make good on his pledge](https://www.tubefilter.com/2018/06/05/jawed-karim-me-at-the-zoo-new-video/) to upload more videos alongside “me at the zoo.” Even if he doesn’t, the first contribution to the platform’s library will continue to speak loudly without saying many words at all.

# 23rd April 2005: The first video uploaded to YouTube is "Me at the zoo"
## Channel: HistoryPod
84.4K subscribers
57 likes

### Description
2,621 views
Posted: 2026-04-22
YouTube had been created earlier in 2005 by three former employees of PayPal. Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim sought to develop a website that allowed users to upload, host, and share videos easily through a web browser. At the time, distributing video online was technically difficult for many users because it required specialised software and large amounts of data storage. The YouTube platform simplified the process by hosting the video files and providing an embedded player that could be viewed directly on the website.

“Me at the zoo” shows Karim speaking in front of the elephant enclosure at the San Diego Zoo in San Diego, California. The video lasts approximately eighteen seconds and contains no special effects or editing. Its informal nature has since been interpreted as representative of the website’s purpose as a whole, which was to allow users to share personal recordings and other types of content.

After its launch, YouTube grew rapidly in popularity. The ability to share links and embed videos on other websites helped the platform spread quickly across the internet. By late 2006 the service had attracted a large audience and was purchased by Google.The video “Me at the zoo” has remained available on YouTube as a record of the platform’s beginnings. Although brief and technically simple, it is often cited as the starting point of a major change in how video content is distributed and viewed online. The upload of 23 April 2005 therefore represents a notable moment in the development of the internet and global digital communication and entertainment.
